newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mideast leaders go to U.S. summit, Arabs wary.
newsitem.headline: Mideast leaders go to U.S. summit, Arabs wary.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and King Hussein of Jordan left for Washington on Monday for a Middle East summit viewed with deep suspicion by other Arab leaders.
A Palestinian official said Palestinian President Yasser Arafat would also go to Washington, despite his request that U.S. President Bill Clinton postpone the meeting from Tuesday.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who shares Arafat's reservations about the summit, held his cards close to his chest. Egyptian officials have not said if he will go.

"He (Arafat) is going now to Luxembourg and then Washington," said the PLO official, who declined to be named. Arafat was to confer with ministers from the European Union, which was not invited to the summit.
He did not say if the United States or Israel had offered Arafat anything to make him change his mind, or even whether Arafat would meet Netanyahu without conditions.
Arafat and Mubarak seemed earlier on Monday to be in revolt against U.S. diplomacy, refusing to rush into a meeting with Netanyahu until they knew what Israel might offer.

"Mubarak wants to see a clearly defined programme of action (by Israel). And he doesn't want to get involved in an unsuccessful summit," said an Arab diplomat close to Monday's talks between Arafat and Mubarak.
"So far the Israelis are still being intransigent. Contacts are continuing but the position is not clear," he added.

Clinton called for the summit after five days of clashes in which 55 Palestinians and 14 Israelis died. The violence began when Israel opened a tunnel near the Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem, Islam's third holiest site.

"The loss of life and the tragedy of the violence in the Middle East this week have been a terrible development for the Israeli and the Palestinian people, a blow to all those who have worked for a lasting peace, an encouragement to those who oppose a lasting peace," Clinton said.

Diplomats say the Arab leaders are concerned that Clinton and Netanyahu will try merely to restore the status quo before the outbreak of violence, without answering Palestinian grievances about the Israeli government's policies.
The Palestinians say Netanyahu's statements in favour of Middle East peace are meant to deceive world opinion while Israel presses on with settling Palestinian areas.
Palestinian officials said an all-night meeting between Palestinians, Israelis, U.S. and U.N. officials failed to solve problems over what the summit would discuss.
Arafat and Mubarak want Israel to close the tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem. Netanyahu says the controversial tunnel will stay open forever and would not be on the agenda.
"The idea was to agree on most everything here before going to Washington, but no conclusions were reached," said Marwan Kanafani, an Arafat aide.

"The Israelis refused to agree on any political issues. They wanted to discuss security issues. They are not serious, and Arafat has no desire to meet Netanyahu just for the sake of meeting him," added a PLO official who declined to be named.
In Washington, U.S. officials appeared to brush aside Palestinian reservations about the summit preparations.
"If we're going to break the cycle of violence, we need a re-engagement of the parties at the highest level, and a delay is not going to produce that," a White House official said.

The White House position was echoed by Dennis Ross, the U.S. coordinator for the Middle East peace talks: "The president issued an invitation to Chairman Arafat. Chairman Arafat agreed to come. We expect him to be here."

Mubarak aired his concerns about short-term pacification policies in an interview with the party newspaper Mayo: "The situation can explode again, as long the agreements and treaties are not implemented," he said.

"The latest events in the Palestinian territories are the natural result of procrastination in carrying out the articles of the agreements and the severe pressure on the economy of the Palestinian people," he added.
"I have warned before and I warn again of a new uprising by the Palestinians if they are in despair or lose hope that they will obtain their rights, as enshrined in charters."

On Monday evening Arafat will meet the "troika" of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg -- the past, present and next holders of the European Union's rotating presidency, Italy, Ireland and the Netherlands.
The snub at not being invited to Washington irritated some European governments, who are the main paymasters of the U.S.-dominated peace process but have been denied a high-profile political role.
